articles.title_orig: Live updates: Spain train crash kills at least 30 as witnesses describe devastating scenes
articles.title_zh: Live updates: Spain train crash kills at least 30 as witnesses describe devastating scenes
articles.content_orig:
Toledo, Spain 1:50 p.m. Oct. 28
A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another and caused a derailment on Wednesday morning near Toledo, Spain, killing at least 30 people, according to the regional government.
The fatal accident, which sent multiple carriages down an embankment, comes after another deadly crash involving the same carriers on a southern line in January that killed 46 people, stunned Spain and created deep doubts about the security of its once-vaunted rail system.
At least 30 people were killed in the Wednesday crash, though that number could rise, said Emiliano García-Page, the president of Castilla-La Mancha. He added that about 80 people were injured, 50 of whom had severe injuries.
The cause of the crash was not clear.
In Spanish news reports, passengers who were in the crash described an awful impact that tossed people from a dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. People crawled out of windows and lay in a nearby field, where local workers, who had heard the crash, rushed to help them with first aid kits and saw the first bodies.
The Adif, Spain’s rail authority, said the trains involved were a “Renfe train and another from the Iryo company, both covering the Madrid-Sevilla route.” Renfe, the national rail provider, reported that high-speed service from Madrid, the nation’s capital, to the southern region of Andalusia was suspended.
Initial reports suggested that the Iryo train was stopped on the tracks, and that the Renfe train barreled into it. Local news outlets reported that there were 397 passengers aboard the Renfe train and about 150 aboard the Iryo train.
Isaac Barrientos, a spokesman for the government’s transportation ministry, said initial reports indicated that two carriages of the Iryo train had derailed.
With early national elections set for the end of November, the crash had the potential to become an issue in an already bitter campaign about the competence of the left-wing government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
“Shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo,” Mr. Sánchez, whose office canceled all scheduled meetings, wrote on social media. “Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations. My affection, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families.”
The conservative opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, quickly voiced his own concern as well.
“I am very concerned about the information we are receiving regarding another train accident,” he wrote on social media. “The priority now is to assist the victims and support their families. My full support goes to the emergency teams working on the ground.”
His Popular Party canceled all its campaign events around the country.
José Bautista contributed reporting from Madrid.
Spain’s Civil Guard said on social media that it had set up offices in Madrid, Seville, Córdoba and Toledo for family members of potential victims. The primary goal is to identify missing persons through the collection of DNA samples, the agency said.
The president of Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano García-Page, confirmed that at least 30 people had been killed in the train crash, a number that may rise. About 80 people were injured, 50 of them, according to Mr. García-Page, with severe injuries.
Blood donation groups in the area of the train crash are urging donors to come to hospitals in Toledo and Ciudad Real to “urgently replenish the reserves. Blood of all types will be needed.”
The fatal train crash near Toledo on Wednesday comes months after a deadly collision in southern Spain that involved the same carriers. In that accident, in January, 46 people were killed when two high-speed trains collided near Adamuz, in the country’s worst rail disaster since 2013.
The crash in January occurred when a train belonging to the private company Iryo derailed as it traveled toward Madrid. The train had been traveling north from Málaga when two of its rear cars fell into the opposite track. Seconds later, a southbound train operated by Spain’s national rail company, Renfe, slammed into the carriages .
The two trains were carrying hundreds of people when the collision occurred. An official report on what caused that accident is not yet available, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause.
The accident shocked Spain and led to deep uncertainty about the safety of the country’s rail system, which contains the world’s second-longest high-speed rail network.
The deadly crash on Wednesday was the third in Spain this year. Days after the accident in January, a commuter train near Barcelona struck a collapsed retaining wall and derailed, killing one person.
Videos shot by passengers after the crash show parts of the derailed carriages pulverized, with charred wheels, and bags and seats strewn across an embankment. Emergency workers tend to the injured or hover over people covered in Mylar blankets. The arid field outside the small towns of Los Yébenes and Urda has become a parking lot of emergency vehicles and tents.
Video filmed inside one of the trains and verified by The New York Times shows smoke rising from a charred, mangled carriage on the slope of the rail line. The footage was first shared by the Spanish radio station Capital Radio, which said an employee had been on one of the trains at the time of the crash.
The first eyewitness reports from the crash are beginning to trickle in on Spanish media. Passengers are describing an awful impact that tossed people from the dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. Passengers crawled out of windows and lay in in a nearby field, where local workers, who heard the crash, rushed to help them with first aid kits and saw the first bodies.
The crash comes months after a deadly collision in January in southern Spain that involved the same carriers. That accident, in which two high-speed trains collided, killing 46 people, was the country’s worst railway disaster since 2013.
An official report on what caused the January crash is not yet available, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause.
Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement that it was deploying a military emergency unit and Civil Guard officers to the scene of the crash in the province of Toledo. Investigators from Spain’s Major Disaster Unit are also en route.

articles.title_orig: Israel Election Results Live Updates: Exit Polls Show No Clear Winner
articles.title_zh: Israel Election Results Live Updates: Exit Polls Show No Clear Winner
articles.content_orig:
Israel’s stock market has fallen sharply amid exit polls showing no clear winner in the country’s parliamentary elections.
The benchmark Tel Aviv 125 index dropped as much as 3.5 percent in early trading on Wednesday as investors weighed the unclear results of Israel’s first election since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza.
Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition nor the opposition bloc headed by Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot appeared on track to gain a parliamentary majority in the 26th Knesset.
With more than 84 percent of votes counted as of 11 GMT, Netanyahu’s coalition was on course to win 54 seats, while Eisenkot’s opposition bloc was headed for 49 seats, according to tallies published by Israeli media.
Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority in the unicameral parliament.
Israel’s economy has been running hot despite being on a war footing for the past three years amid an influx of investment in the local tech sector.
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 2.9 percent in 2025 and 3.2 percent in the first half of 2026, according to government figures.
The Bank of Israel last week raised its GDP growth forecast for all of 2026 to 5.6 percent, up from 4 percent, citing ramped-up production by Israeli firms overseas.
The central bank has forecast that GDP growth for 2027 would reach 7.5 percent, far surpassing estimates for advanced economies such as the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and Japan.

articles.title_orig: Why China is desperate to ship cars outside of the country
articles.title_zh: Why China is desperate to ship cars outside of the country
articles.content_orig:
To understand why China is desperate to ship cars overseas, visit a dealership in Beijing.
Autumn has traditionally been the peak time to buy vehicles in the country, but this year many showrooms are empty or shut.
Car salesman Li Ke said that other than the Covid-19 pandemic, the 2026 "golden September and silver October" season, as it's known, is the slowest he's seen in his 26 years on the job.
"In past years, customers would come to the showrooms nonstop," he told CNBC during an interview in his deserted showroom at a complex of dealerships on the outskirts of the Chinese capital. "We would have deals to sign every day. But nowadays we see only two to three deals a week. It's a dramatic drop."
Many people in China aren't buying cars because an unstable job market and a continued slide in property prices have undercut consumer confidence. The government has also scaled back incentives such as cash-for-clunkers subsidies and tax breaks to go electric, car salespeople said.
Passenger car retail sales for 2026 in China totaled 13.33 million units through September, falling 21.7% from a year ago, according to the China Passenger Car Association. For the full year 2026, China's domestic passenger car retail sales are set to fall 22% to 18.5 million vehicles, the association said — under the level recorded in the first year of the pandemic.
Even electric vehicles, which were once a bright spot, are down. Gasoline car sales have been declining in China because of the country's transition to electric vehicles, but sales in China of new-energy vehicles — which includes EVs — dropped by 12.8% from January through September.
"Customers are watching every penny," Li said. "When looking at all the new functions on all these new models, they are weighing what is most practical, economic and worth their money over the long term. We don't see impulse buying. Because of the bad economy, people are taking more time to replace their cars."
The fierce competition has led to bruising price wars in recent years, a key reason Chinese carmakers have cast their eyes overseas and why Beijing is fearful of partners like the U.S. and Europe putting up coordinated trade barriers against its massive car exports, analysts said.
Industrial profits for the first nine months of the year were up 15.5% from the same period in 2025, but September showed signs of weakness relative to the prior eight months, according to China's National Bureau of Statistics . For the auto manufacturing industry specifically, profits from January to September shrank by 22.8% compared with last year.
To preserve cash, Li's dealership moved out of a pricey streetside space to one with less foot traffic but that rents at a fraction of the cost.
With profit margins eroding, Li said he sees little point in offering further discounts. He said the bigger hurdle is the prevailing Chinese consumer attitude toward big-ticket purchases.
"Chinese buyers would rather wait," he said.

articles.title_orig: Iran sees only unacceptable ideas in latest mediation to end war, official says
articles.title_zh: Iran sees only unacceptable ideas in latest mediation to end war, official says
articles.content_orig:
The United States has told its Gulf allies to prepare for a brief but intense campaign against Iran after the midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on the matter.
The U.S. military is shipping a Patriot antimissile system from Texas to Israel and has transferred troops off bases where they may have been vulnerable, officials familiar with the decisions told the outlet.
American forces across the Middle East have been restocking munitions and aircraft have been preparing for strikes, the paper reported, while an additional aircraft carrier strike group and Marine unit are set to join the 20 or so warships in the region, though some other vessels could be withdrawn.
The Houthis have called on people in Aden International Airport in southern Yemen to evacuate immediately, claiming that a Saudi military cargo aircraft is transporting weapons there intended to kill Yemenis.
Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said in a post on X : "Our armed forces call on those present at Aden Airport to evacuate the airport immediately, due to the presence of an enemy Saudi military cargo aircraft transporting weapons to kill the sons of the Yemeni people."
Aden is the seat of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, and has been since the Iran-backed Houthis took the country's capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
A senior Iranian official denied Wednesday that Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal, saying instead that Qatar had come with "unacceptable" ideas, the Reuters news agency reported.
Reuters reported earlier Wednesday that Qatari mediators handed Iran a new draft deal to end the war on Sunday, citing an official briefed on the negotiations.
Dismissing the idea that they had been given a new peace proposal, the Iranian official speaking to the news agency said Tehran would show no flexibility on the nuclear issue.
Qatari mediators on Sunday handed Iran a new draft deal to end the war, the Reuters news agency reported, citing an official briefed on the negotiations.
Tehran is considering the proposal and set to respond by the end of the week, the agency reported Wednesday.
The source added that there were concerns in Tehran before the meeting on Sunday that Israel could resume its bombardment of Iran this week.
The cost of the Iran war has risen to an estimated $47 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. military's Central Command obtained by CBS News Tuesday.
Like previous estimates, it does not include damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East. The bulk of the cost, $29 billion, is for replacing expended munitions.
According to a report released by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office in September, the Iran war could cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues.
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition in Tuesday's election, but his Likud party still emerged as the largest party among all the contenders. Neither bloc, Netanyahu or the opposition, has a clear majority.
While Netanyahu appears to have won fewer votes than his main challenger, according to the early exit polls, both candidates will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.
One or the other would need to obtain majority support in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.
Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.
Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 futures inch higher ahead of Fed decision. Nasdaq futures gain after SK Hynix profit boom: Live updates
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 futures inch higher ahead of Fed decision. Nasdaq futures gain after SK Hynix profit boom: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures were mixed on Wednesday as investors awaited a rate policy decision from the Federal Reserve due Wednesday and earnings reports from mega-cap technology companies.
S&P 500 futures added 0.2%, and Nasdaq-100 futures rose 0.3%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were down 21 points, or 0.04%.
Focus will turn to domestic monetary policy as the Fed wraps up its two-day policy meeting. The central bank is widely predicted to keep interest rates steady at a target rate range of 3.75% to 4%. Policymakers raised rates by a quarter percentage point at their September meeting .
According to CME's FedWatch tool , there's a roughly 90% chance that the Fed maintains the current interest rate, but some expect that Chairman Kevin Warsh will signal that more hikes are coming in future policy meetings. The decision on interest rates will be announced at 2 p.m. ET.
U.S. chipmakers moved higher in premarket trading Wednesday, buoyed by SK Hynix posting record quarterly profit — a development that sent U.S. shares of the South Korean chipmaker up nearly 8%. Micron Technology was up 4%, while Arm Holdings advanced 2%. Intel and Marvell Technology each added almost 2%, as did Advanced Micro Devices .
Investors' attention will remain on the artificial intelligence trade after the bell, as "Magnificent Seven" giants Alphabet and Microsoft will kick off Big Tech earnings. The former was last seen up more than 1%, while the latter was down marginally.
Tech stocks, particularly those with exposure to the AI buildout, have struggled in recent weeks amid questions over the technology's financing . However, Morgan Stanley's chief U.S. equity strategist, Mike Wilson , thinks that the recent recovery in tech stocks is a sign that the trend may be nearing its end.
"Most of the correction is already over," he said in an appearance on CNBC's " Closing Bell " on Tuesday. "We've been in correction mode for four or five months... the market I think has digested this very efficiently."
Across the Atlantic, the pan-European Stoxx 600 shed 0.27%. The U.K. FTSE 100 fell 0.33%, France's CAC 40 dropped 0.13%, and Germany's DAX lost 0.11%.  In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 1.08% higher and South Korea's Kospi rose 6.63%. Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 was flat. Mainland China's CSI 300 closed 0.85% higher.
Wendy's surged as much as 16% in the premarket Wednesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that Nelson Peltz's Trian Management has offered to pay $1.4 billion to take the fast food chain private.
The activist firm, a long time shareholder in Wendy's, is leading the deal with other partners including investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter.
U.S. stocks were active before Wednesday's opening bell as earnings and acquisition news drove sharp moves across several stocks.
Ultralife surged after agreeing to a $320 million acquisition by EnerSys, while SK hynix climbed on record AI-memory earnings. Robinhood fell as weaker crypto activity weighed on its quarterly results, and Enphase Energy dropped following declining revenue and continued pressure in residential solar.
Read more here on stocks making the biggest moves premarket.
Shares for Robinhood fell more than 6% after the brokerage's net income fell to $468 million from $556 million from the year before.
Robinhood reported 51 cents per share in its third-quarter earnings, below expectations from analysts polled by LSEG consensus with 56 cents per share. The brokerage reported $1.42 billion in revenue, in line with analysts' consensus.
The company's reported transaction-based revenue of $867 million also came fell short of expectations from StreetAccount's $879 million.
Cheesecake Factory shares dipped more than 2%, even after its latest earnings exceeded expectations on the top and bottom lines.
The restaurant chain and distributor of specialty cheesecakes posted third quarter earnings of $1.02 per share, excluding items, on revenues of $1.03 billion. Analysts surveyed by LSEG had expected per-share earnings of 95 cents on revenues of $1.00 billion.
The stock was already running hot into the print. Shares are up more than 110% year to date, and have rallied more than 20% just over the last three months.
Mortgage rates fell for the second straight week, and that finally brought consumers back to their brokers. A growing share, however, applied for riskier loans at even lower rates.
Total mortgage application volume rose 3.4% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, decreased to 7.37% from 7.41%, with points increasing to 0.76 from 0.75, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. Read more .
Treasury yields moved higher as investors awaited the Federal Reserve's latest monetary policy decision, due later in the session.
The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 1 basis point higher at 5.0092% by 5:40 a.m. E.T.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, was flat at 4.7453%.
The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasurys — which tend to move on geopolitical events — was up by more than 1 basis point at 5.3157%.
UniCredit chairman Pier Carlo Padoan will step down at the end of his term for personal reasons, the Italian bank said Wednesday.
Padoan — who served as Italy's finance and economy minister from 2014 to 2018 — has been chair of UniCredit's board since April 2021.
In a statement, UniCredit said Padoan had steered the bank through an "operational and strategic transformation", navigating "challenging circumstances arising from both the broader macroeconomic environment and the evolving political landscape."
The bank said Padoan will work with its nomination committee to identify a successor.
UniCredit's Milan-listed shares were last seen around 0.5% lower in morning trade.
European equities were trading mixed on Wednesday morning, as investors digested a swathe of corporate earnings out of the region.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was marginally lower by 9:15 a.m. in London (4:15 a.m. ET), with the FTSE 100 down by 0.2% while the CAC 40 added 0.1% and Germany's DAX was little changed.
Autos stocks led regional gains after earnings from Jeep maker Stellantis , Mercedes-Benz and Porsche , while banking stocks fell after reports from Santander , UBS , Deutsche Bank and BNP Paribas .
Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 1.08% higher at 63,954.19,  while the Topix slipped 0.14% at 3,991.71.
South Korea's Kospi rose 6.63% to 6,012.44 and the tech-focused, small-cap Kosdaq advanced 3.69% at 771.28.
Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 ended flat at 8,847.30.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 0.24% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 closed 0.85% higher at 4,083.87.
GSK posted quarterly earnings slightly ahead of forecasts early Wednesday, as the drugmaker continues to advance its pipeline ahead of a looming patent cliff which will see revenue drop for older, best-selling medicines as they come to face generic competition.
Third-quarter sales came in at £8.9 billion ($11.8 billion), up 5% year-on-year in constant exchange rates.
Operating profit in the quarter fell 16%, driven by restructuring charges of £328 million. On an adjusted basis, operating profit grew by 5% to £3.1 billion.
The London-listed company reiterated its full-year guidance and said it remained on track for 2031 sales of more than £40 billion.
On Tuesday, GSK's oncology lead told the Wall Street Journal it would nearly double the number of cancer medicines in its pipeline next year, as Britain's second-largest drugmaker bets big on the unit under CEO Luke Miels.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Nelson Peltz’s Trian Offers to Buy Wendy’s for $1.4 Billion
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Nelson Peltz’s Trian Offers to Buy Wendy’s for $1.4 Billion
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wendy's ( WEN ) may be cooking up burgers for a billionaire soon.
Longtime Wendy's investor and former chairman Nelson Peltz of Trian Partners has reportedly offered $1.4 billion to buy the struggling fast food giant, according to an SEC filing.
Wendy's shares rose 15% in premarket trading. The company's market cap was $1.17 billion prior to the deal.
A Wendy's spokesperson didn't return a request for comment. A spokesperson for Trian Partners didn't return a request for comment.
Billionaire Peltz — while familiar with the operations — would essentially be buying a dumpster fire.
After nearly two years of struggles competing with the likes of behemoths McDonald's ( MCD ) and Yum! Brands' ( YUM ) Taco Bell, plus upstarts such as Shake Shack ( SHAK ), Wendy's is on the cusp of a large number of restaurant closures.
"With one of its largest franchisees filing bankruptcy in September (although contested by WEN given prior termination of franchise agreement), we think investors likely expect closures to tick higher than expected, but we admit visibility on our side remains somewhat limited and there could still be a range of outcomes," veteran restaurant analyst Andy Barish warned in a recent note.
"That said," he added, "given our view that there are likely additional franchise operators in the system facing challenges with leveraged balance sheets, higher interest rates and profitability pressures from higher beef, labor & build costs (like many others in QSR), we think it is prudent to moderate our development estimates and bake in more potential closures over the next 6-12 months, as the company works to strengthen its system."
Meritage Hospitality Group, one of Wendy's largest franchise operators, with more than 300 locations, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September following severe margin pressures and an escalating dispute with corporate headquarters. The company reportedly initiated plans to shutter at least 41 locations. Reports emerged this week that it could close up to 60.
The high-profile bankruptcy only added grease to the smoldering fire that is the Wendy's restaurant base.
Franchisees had already been closing their locations and heading for the hills.
Buried inside Wendy's brutal second quarter earnings call was a mention that 289 locations closed in the US during the first half of the year.
There are about 5,700 Wendy's in the US, and Barish estimated the Wendy's US store base will be around 5,600 by the end of 2027.
The decision on how many more locations will be closed falls on new CEO Bob Wright, who hasn't hidden his view that Wendy's needs to focus on more profitable locations.
Wright officially took over as CEO on May 21, adding to the yawning list of executive turnover at the fast food chain over the past two years. He is a seasoned fast food exec who spent the previous five years fixing Potbelly as CEO. Wright's appointment marked a return to Wendy's, where he previously served in several senior leadership roles, including COO.
Wright has his work cut out for him in saving Wendy's beyond tightening up the store base count.
Wendy's has posted six straight quarters of same-store sales declines, per Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace analysis.

articles.title_orig: Amazon relaxes push for AI use as Anthropic reveals shocking stats
articles.title_zh: Amazon relaxes push for AI use as Anthropic reveals shocking stats
articles.content_orig:
An Amazon memo published Tuesday encouraged its software engineers to stop "tokenmaxxing" and start being more judicious about how they are using AI to accomplish tasks this week.
The memo, circulated within Amazon last month but made public on Tuesday, argued that AI token usage and code generation are "deeply flawed" metrics for measuring productivity.
“We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes,” the company wrote.
“We’re just seeing the beginning of AI’s effect on software engineering,” the company wrote. “While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there’s a lot that’s still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice.”
Major companies have struggled to square the massive cost of AI usage while the benefits of using the technology are often hard to measure at a large scale.
President Donald Trump vowed to ban the term "artificial intelligence" as news outlets and other sources have been slow to take up his newly-invented term "super intelligence."
Trump announced the plan in a post on his Truth Social account, reacting to an article from The Wall Street Journal that discussed artificial intelligence.
"When will The Wall Street Journal start calling Artificial Intelligence (AI), a very bad and inaccurate name, SI (Super Intelligence), the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be. In short order, we will be officially BANNING the term, 'AI/Artificial Intelligence,' in all relevant documents, and everything else, due to its inaccuracy," Trump wrote.
It is unclear how Trump plans to pursue a ban on the term, however.
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic's IPO filing is drawing scrutiny over what it leaves out about the potential impact of AI on American workers, despite the company's repeated warnings that the technology could disrupt white-collar employment.
Axios senior AI reporter Madison Mills pointed out Tuesday that Anthropic's filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission discusses the reputational and regulatory risks associated with concerns about AI replacing workers but does not explicitly address whether widespread job losses could hurt its own business.
"For all the warnings about AI replacing knowledge workers, Anthropic's IPO filing barely addresses job displacement, and says nothing about what mass unemployment could mean for its own business," Mills wrote on X.
Mills noted that the word "jobs" appears just five times in the filing, with three references focused on how public concerns about AI's impact on employment could damage Anthropic's reputation, invite regulation or slow adoption of its technology.
The company estimates that knowledge work represents more than $40 trillion in global economic value, positioning AI as a tool to boost productivity and economic growth rather than projecting how widespread adoption could affect employment.
Fox News' Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.
The apparent omission is notable given Anthropic's own research into workplace disruption. In a report published earlier this month, the company found that its share of junior technical hires had declined as AI agents increasingly took over coding and other tasks.
Anthropic is expanding its agreement with the federal government's General Services Administration, granting federal users a 40% discount on many of its services.
The discount applies to Claude Enterprise, Claude for Government, the Claude API, and "every product surface, including when agencies buy from us directly today and through cloud providers in the coming months."
The discount also extends to state, local, tribal and territorial governments. Anthropic says.
"We are also launching a dedicated program to help agencies implement and make the most of their Claude use. These programs are commonly leveraged by our private sector customers and we’re looking forward to bringing those best practices to our public sector partners in the coming weeks," Anthropic wrote.
"Approximately 500 US federal, state, and local government organizations now use Claude. Weekly Claude for Government active users are up about eightfold since February, and usage across federal civilian agencies has grown about 20-fold in a year. Those organizations run some of the most important systems in the country, usually on tight budgets and with long procurement cycles. This agreement is built to support that work, so they can apply Claude to hard problems without a large upfront commitment," it added.
Anthropic released a study on Tuesday finding that a large majority of professional statistical analysts deferred to AI when crunching data and presented the AI's judgement as their own.
The study tasked 50 professional analysts with using Claude code to scrutinize a farming cooperative and recommend whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded.
The analysts were required to make four choices between two reasonable options during the process, but Anthropic did not inform them that the Claude code they were using would be biased in favor of one of those options based on a coin flip.
"The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead," Anthropic wrote.
"Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed," it continued.
"Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment," Anthropic added.
Covered by: Anders Hagstrom

articles.title_orig: They bought cabins to live on a luxury cruise ship. High fuel costs got them kicked off in Cambodia.
articles.title_zh: They bought cabins to live on a luxury cruise ship. High fuel costs got them kicked off in Cambodia.
articles.content_orig:
Morning Rundown: Deadlock in Israeli election, Trump fights for votes in Texas, and the threat of drug-resistant germs
A residential cruise ship halted operations in Cambodia on Tuesday amid soaring fuel costs , leaving passengers in limbo after the U.S. company that operates it ordered them to disembark.
Florida-based Villa Vie Residences said in a news release that it was working to identify “temporary living arrangements” for people aboard The Odyssey, a 642-foot cruise ship that launched from Belfast, Northern Ireland, three years ago and promised passengers “an unparalleled lifestyle of luxury and exploration” as it toured the planet.
Cabins on The Odyssey were for sale or rent.
According to the company , the ship can accommodate 650 residents. A Cambodian official said Wednesday there were 203 passengers and 156 ​crew members on the ship. Some passengers had already departed on ​flights, while others were waiting in the port city of Sihanoukville, Long Dimanche, deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk Province, told media.
The ship is scheduled to refuel before leaving ‌Cambodia on ⁠Saturday, he added.
An executive with the company, Mikael Petterson, declined to provide additional details in an email to NBC News. In a release this year announcing the company’s second residential cruise ship, Petterson said The Odyssey was 85% sold.
The company said in Tuesday’s release that it had taken significant measures to reduce fuel consumption but that those steps had failed to offset the spike in costs.
Global oil prices have surged since the war with Iran began this year, disrupting the world’s flow of fuel. In recent days, oil prices have climbed to their highest levels in months.
“Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution,” the company said. “Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees while we work toward restructuring and recapitalization over the next 60 days. That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured.”
Randy Cassingham, a resident on the boat, wrote in a blog post that he learned his journey was over after a company official posted a note on a message board for the ship shortly after 7 a.m. Monday.
The Odyssey was entering a “temporary lay up” period — indicating it would no longer be used — and everyone had to disembark by 2 p.m., the message said, according to Cassingham, who runs ResidentialCruising.com and didn’t immediately reply to an interview request.
Cassingham attributed the development to a “cascade of problems” that he would detail later.
Pamela Reckamp, who rented a cabin with her husband and disembarked this month, said in an interview that she wasn’t surprised that the ship’s journey was over.
Reckamp, 59, recalled having attended a meeting in early September at which a company official asked cabin owners to help them raise $1 million so they could leave Ha Long Bay, Vietnam.
“She said, ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp recalled. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’”
When the ship’s financial issues were raised during another meeting a few weeks later, Reckamp recalled, a woman stood up and said she’d bought a cabin in August and hadn’t been made aware of the issues.
“I sold my house,” Reckamp recalled the woman saying. “I sold my car. I bought my home on this ship.”
Reckamp said she felt terrible for the residents and the staff, who she said were lovely.
“We dodged a bullet,” she added.
Villa Vie Residences didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday night.
In a lawsuit filed last year, a company that bought a cabin on The Odyssey for $469,000 accused Villa Vie Residences of fraud, alleging it misrepresented its financial stability.
The company’s business model was not financially sound, the suit alleges, “but rather precarious.”
The plaintiffs are asking for a jury trial and unspecified damages of more than $100,000. Villa Vie Residences denied the allegations in the suit, which is ongoing.
Other cabins on the ship were available for significantly less money. Even though 85% of the ship was sold, the company said in 2024, prospective residents could still “secure their dream home starting at just $119,000.”
“When we launched Odyssey, we set out to prove that residential cruising wasn’t just possible — it was sustainable,” Petterson said in July.
Tim Stelloh is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

Warhammer Age of Sigmar: October Update
New rules updates are going live for Warhammer Age of Sigmar – read on to see if they affect your army.
Major changes: Khazalite Holds, Sons of Behemat
Minor changes: Ogor Mawtribes, Lumineth Realm-lords, Skaven, Sylvaneth, Nighthaunt
With the advent of new battletomes, a few older rules needed a quick update to stay relevant – namely where keywords were involved. The Khazalite Holds in particular see a lot of older FYRESLAYERS keywords turned into the new GRIMMDRON ,* so things like the Fyreslayers Scourge of Aqshy rules can still be used.
As well as having their keywords changed, the Lofnir Drothkeepers Army of Renown has also been rewritten slightly to better fit their new rules. Notably, it now includes an additional way to generate grudge marks when your Magmadroths are killed.
The Sons of Behemat previously struggled to field game-legal 2,000 point Armies of Renown without needing to dip into Auxiliaries, so now they have a new option to field regiments led by Mancrusher Gargants.** This applies for both the Matriarch’s Mob and Stomper Tribe , so now’s a great time to give their new options a go.
Besides these two larger updates, a few fixes and clarifications have been added to several factions, such as the Skaven’s Verminlord Corruptor having its points corrected after a typo in the last update – one that most of you caught onto anyway, but a slip-up nonetheless! Some units like Pyregheists and Ydrilan Riverblades can also now double up their Champions when reinforced, like other, similar warscrolls. If your faction of choice is listed under minor changes , have a quick look for their updates with the New tag (or search for the ✹ icon).
Minor changes: Daughters of Khaine Heartflayer Troupe, Nighthaunt Slasher Host, Orruk Warclans Swampskulka Gang, Seraphon Sunblood Prowlers
This is one of the largest Spearhead updates we’ve had for a while, with a handful of ability clarifications that add the ‘Once Per Turn (Army)’ condition to bring them in line with other factions. Otherwise, it’s business as usual in the Spearhead arena, so get out into the City of Ash and show those scuttling Skaven miscreants what for.
Download the latest changes, enjoy your battles in the Mortal Realms, and if you have anything you need answered, make sure to send your questions to AoSFAQ@gwplc.com .

articles.title_orig: Touchscreen MacBook Pro to Debut Today With These 5 Features
articles.title_zh: Touchscreen MacBook Pro to Debut Today With These 5 Features
articles.content_orig:
Some reports have suggested the new high-end MacBook Pro models that Apple is expected to announce today might not be called ‌MacBook Pro‌s at all. They could in fact be something altogether new and more exciting – " MacBook Ultra ," perhaps – marketed as the company's top-tier laptop offering. The machines are expected to sit above the current M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros, rather than replace them, suggesting the latter will remain in Apple's lineup.
One thing to state up front is that Apple is expected to stick with the existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for its touchscreen MacBook models. Apple reportedly plans to skip what would have been the "M6 Pro" and "M6 Max" for more powerful "M7 Pro" and "M7 Max" chips. Apple announced the new entry-level 14-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌ with the M6 chip yesterday, ahead of pre-orders opening today, but the first "MacBook Ultra" models will use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, after which second-generation models will come with M7 Pro and Max chips in late 2027.
Apple has already unveiled most of a second set of new products this week, as MacRumors ' sources earlier indicated: the OLED iPad mini arrived on Monday, and the M6 iMac and M6 14-inch MacBook Pro followed yesterday. The new touchscreen models are expected to debut today at Apple's "Pro and tell" event in Los Angeles and become available for pre-order at 10:10 a.m. Pacific Time, with Bloomberg reporting that availability could begin as early as November 6. Recent reports have referred to the machines simply as new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models, so the final name remains uncertain.
Below, we've listed the features and changes we are expecting for the new high-end MacBook Pro models.
Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo say Apple is readying OLED technology for these models, and industry reports corroborate their claims. Samsung Display is said to be making the panels exclusively , and the supplier has invested heavily in an 8.6-generation OLED production line in South Korea. The line reached a key milestone for mass production in May.
OLED presents an overall upgrade over the current mini-LED display technology, bringing deeper colors and a higher contrast ratio with true blacks. In an OLED display, individual pixels turn off instead of dimming when not activated, so there's less light leakage and better power efficiency. OLED displays also tend to have better HDR output than mini-LED, but they don't always match mini-LED brightness levels.
The new ‌MacBook Pro‌ is expected to become the first Mac to support touch input directly on the display. It's a notable shift from Apple's longstanding position against bringing touchscreen functionality to the Mac.
Apple previously experimented with touch controls through the OLED Touch Bar on earlier ‌MacBook Pro‌ models, but the feature was ultimately discontinued following a lukewarm reception. Rather than positioning the ‌MacBook Pro‌ as a touch-centric device like the ‌iPad‌, Apple is reportedly planning to let users move seamlessly between touch and traditional trackpad or mouse input across the system.
There are features in ‌macOS Golden Gate‌ that hint at a future touchscreen Mac. Apple added direct touch input to Sidecar so users can tap and interact with macOS elements when using the ‌iPad‌ as a Mac display. macOS Golden Gate‌ also supports an iPhone-style pull-to-refresh option, and it can be used across apps like Safari, Mail, News, Podcasts, and Calendar. A pull-to-refresh option makes the most sense on a touch display.
Apple has reportedly developed a reinforced hinge and screen hardware to prevent the display from bouncing back or moving when touched. Apple is apparently aware of the same issue that plagues existing touch PCs.
Gurman has reported that Apple is working to make the OLED MacBook Pro thinner , as part of the company's plan to create "the thinnest and lightest products in their categories across the whole tech industry." (Think the latest iPad Pro and iPad Air – two of the thinnest devices the company has ever made.) Indeed, the reporter said there's a good chance that the next MacBook Pro model will represent a "true overhaul" for the laptop, thanks to the combination of the OLED display and thinner design.
In October 2025, Gurman reported that the OLED MacBook Pro models would have "thinner and lighter" frames. Then again in November 2025 , he said the touchscreen models would have "a thinner chassis."
However, Gurman has walked back somewhat on his previous reporting that Apple's upcoming touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro will be thinner than current models. "I don't think it'll be significantly thinner in the end," he said in early October 2026.
In a last-minute detail, Gurman reports that Apple has also reworked the cooling system to improve airflow through the hinge while helping to reduce the laptop's weight.
The MacBook Ultra could ditch the current notch used in the MacBook Pro models for a display cutout potentially similar to the iPhone's Dynamic Island, according to Bloomberg . Such a move would mirror Apple's iPhone evolution, since the iPhone's notch became the current Dynamic Island starting with the iPhone 14 Pro models in 2022.
As with the iPhone‌, the Mac ‌Dynamic Island‌ will be interactive and it will contextually expand based on the app or Mac feature in use. The change should address long-standing user complaints about the notch, which physically ingresses into the macOS menu bar.
There is no doubt that Apple will unveil the new MacBook Pro models as ultra-premium products carrying price tags that are higher than the current MacBook Pro 14-inch and 16-inch models. Apple increased the prices of all its Macs in June 2026 – MacBook Pro‌ pricing went up $300 – so the "MacBook Ultra" will likely be even more expensive than expected. ‌
For what it's worth, the higher-end 14-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌ with M5 Pro chip starts at $2,499 after the price increase, while the 16-inch M5 Pro ‌MacBook Pro‌ starts at $2,999. More specifically, Bloomberg reported this week that Apple has discussed charging $2,899 for the new 14-inch model with an M5 Pro chip, which would mean a starting price of at least $3,399 for the 16-inch model. Hold onto your wallets!

articles.title_orig: China’s Electric Carmakers Are Running Out of Domestic Buyers | The 10-Point for Oct. 28
articles.title_zh: China’s Electric Carmakers Are Running Out of Domestic Buyers | The 10-Point for Oct. 28
articles.content_orig:
To understand why China is desperate to ship cars overseas, visit a dealership in Beijing.
Autumn has traditionally been the peak time to buy vehicles in the country, but this year many showrooms are empty or shut.
Car salesman Li Ke said that other than the Covid-19 pandemic, the 2026 "golden September and silver October" season, as it's known, is the slowest he's seen in his 26 years on the job.
"In past years, customers would come to the showrooms nonstop," he told CNBC during an interview in his deserted showroom at a complex of dealerships on the outskirts of the Chinese capital. "We would have deals to sign every day. But nowadays we see only two to three deals a week. It's a dramatic drop."
Many people in China aren't buying cars because an unstable job market and a continued slide in property prices have undercut consumer confidence. The government has also scaled back incentives such as cash-for-clunkers subsidies and tax breaks to go electric, car salespeople said.
Passenger car retail sales for 2026 in China totaled 13.33 million units through September, falling 21.7% from a year ago, according to the China Passenger Car Association. For the full year 2026, China's domestic passenger car retail sales are set to fall 22% to 18.5 million vehicles, the association said — under the level recorded in the first year of the pandemic.
Even electric vehicles, which were once a bright spot, are down. Gasoline car sales have been declining in China because of the country's transition to electric vehicles, but sales in China of new-energy vehicles — which includes EVs — dropped by 12.8% from January through September.
"Customers are watching every penny," Li said. "When looking at all the new functions on all these new models, they are weighing what is most practical, economic and worth their money over the long term. We don't see impulse buying. Because of the bad economy, people are taking more time to replace their cars."
The fierce competition has led to bruising price wars in recent years, a key reason Chinese carmakers have cast their eyes overseas and why Beijing is fearful of partners like the U.S. and Europe putting up coordinated trade barriers against its massive car exports, analysts said.
Industrial profits for the first nine months of the year were up 15.5% from the same period in 2025, but September showed signs of weakness relative to the prior eight months, according to China's National Bureau of Statistics . For the auto manufacturing industry specifically, profits from January to September shrank by 22.8% compared with last year.
To preserve cash, Li's dealership moved out of a pricey streetside space to one with less foot traffic but that rents at a fraction of the cost.
With profit margins eroding, Li said he sees little point in offering further discounts. He said the bigger hurdle is the prevailing Chinese consumer attitude toward big-ticket purchases.
"Chinese buyers would rather wait," he said.

articles.title_orig: Amazon warehouse workers tell us what they really think about their new robot coworkers
articles.title_zh: Amazon warehouse workers tell us what they really think about their new robot coworkers
articles.content_orig:
Your browser does not support the video element.
Your browser does not support the video element.
Amazon warehouse workers used to spend much of their days walking, pushing carts through long aisles to manually retrieve customer orders from shelves.
Today, hundreds of "Hercules" robots do this instead, carrying towering yellow storage pods filled with inventory to employee workstations.
"I'd walk like 10 miles a day on average," said Mohammed Khan, who started as an entry-level picker 12 years ago and is now a senior manager at an Amazon warehouse in Tracy, California.
Amazon's robots "cut down all that walking time," he told Business Insider during a recent tour of the facility.
This site is ground zero for a wave of automation that's beginning to wash over the industry. The warehouse and logistics sectors have been powerful sources of job growth since Amazon kicked off the e-commerce revolution 30 years ago, as Business Insider's award-winning Warehouse Nation series revealed in 2022.
If robots automate many warehouse tasks, this powerful engine of job growth could grind to a halt, wiping out thousands of positions and countless opportunities for future workers.
Amazon says employees are being retrained to do more valuable work, such as managing and maintaining robots. Will these new jobs be enough to cover what might be lost? Or could we actually end up with more or better jobs?
Business Insider went looking for answers inside the giant facility in Tracy, a city in California's Central Valley where suburban neighborhoods give way to open farmland.
Across 1.4 million square feet — the equivalent of 23 football fields — robots with names like Hercules, Robin, Cardinal, Pegasus, and Proteus move inventory and sort packages. But they don't run the warehouse alone. Human workers still pick and pack orders, load trucks, and intervene when automated systems fail.
Jobs have not disappeared, but they're changing. Machines increasingly handle work that once required employees to walk miles and lift boxes, while workers monitor and troubleshoot them. The Tracy site employs more than 3,000, up from roughly 1,000 when it opened in 2023, an Amazon spokesperson told Business Insider.
"They're autonomous to an extent," Khan said of his robot counterparts. "They still need a lot of help and maintenance and oversight."
An Amazon spokesperson said rising customer demand drove the facility's workforce growth and that robots help workers process more packages safely and efficiently rather than simply replacing them.
Amazon's more automated, next-generation fulfillment centers are about 25% more productive and cut order-processing time by as much as 25%. And these sites support roughly 30% more skilled jobs in areas including reliability, maintenance, and engineering.
One of the workers now doing that kind of job is Briana Brager.
She joined Amazon about two years ago as an entry-level employee after spending years caring for her family. She had no prior experience in a traditional workplace.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Today, she's a process assistant who helps oversee the warehouse's robotic systems. When a chute jams or a robot stops working, she coordinates the response to keep packages moving.
"The robots do a lot, but we still have to maintain them," she said.
Brager began as a picker before moving into a specialized role supporting robotic-floor operations. She got two weeks of intensive training, followed by additional job shadowing, to learn how to work safely around the equipment. Her current job is less physically demanding than her previous one, she said.
Her role is informally known as the "quarterback" position. She monitors fleets of robots and dispatches employees when a machine needs intervention.
"We call the shots," Brager said.
At the Tracy warehouse, humans and robots move orders together from storage to the loading dock. Employees stow individual items in fabric inventory pods, which Hercules robots carry to pick stations. Workers retrieve the items, then pack and label them.
Robin, a large robotic arm, picks finished packages off a conveyor and places them on small Pegasus mobile robots. Pegasus carries the packages to staging areas alongside other orders headed to the same destination. Cardinal then loads the sorted orders into carts, and Proteus ferries the carts toward outbound trucks.
Khan, the warehouse manager, said workers performed Robin's task manually until a few years ago. They handled packages one at a time, checked them for damage, scanned them, and fed them into the sorting system. He estimated that one Robin can perform roughly the work of two to seven people doing that process manually.
Amazon said that when it introduces systems such as Robin, employees take on other work at the site, including operating robots, clearing jams, monitoring the robotic floor and quality control, and maintenance engineering.
Proteus offers a clear example of how these new warehouse jobs are taking shape. Amazon brought the robots to Tracy last year.
Unlike Hercules, which operates in fenced-off areas, Proteus can move through spaces shared with people. There are roughly 200 of the robots at the Tracy facility, Amazon said.
Before Proteus arrived, workers manually pushed carts filled with packages to the loading dock. Now the robots pick up full carts, carry them to staging areas near the dock, and retrieve empty carts for the return trip.
Some employees who once moved those carts now work as "ground-floor monitors," Amazon said. Instead of spending their shifts moving packages, they respond when a Proteus reports a fault. If the problem is simple, they can reset the robot; otherwise, human maintenance staff take over.
Some workers trained in these jobs have gone on to Amazon's mechatronics apprenticeship program, which can lead to more technical maintenance work.
For all the robots moving through the Tracy warehouse, people remain essential when automation breaks down.
Amazon calls one such destination the "jackpot." When an item loses its routing information while moving through the facility, the automated system sends it to this area, which works a bit like a lost-and-found for packages.
Here, a human worker must determine where the wayward package belongs and return it to the correct flow. "It will require manual intervention," an Amazon representative said.
Other situations require human judgment, too. Products can fall from storage pods and inventory can be damaged or mislabeled. Packing individual products into boxes and loading them onto delivery vehicles are tasks that also remain heavily dependent on people.
This helps explain why even a highly automated Amazon warehouse still employs thousands of workers. The company said it needs people for new packing stations as well as roles across the facility that keep operations running safely and efficiently.
By the time packages get to the loading dock at the Tracy facility, the robots are gone. At least for now.
A person loads each trailer. Amazon uses equipment that extends into the trailer and adjusts to a worker's height, reducing bending and back-and-forth walking. But workers still arrange the packages themselves, trying to fill the trailer to use as much of the space as possible.
"It's a lot of Tetris," one Amazon representative said.
Amazon is already exploring how to automate this task, though. As Business Insider previously reported, Project Tetromino aims to use AI and robotics to automate sorting and vehicle loading at delivery stations, where the work has long remained stubbornly manual.
But that vision remains a work in progress. Amazon's machines can carry shelves, sort packages, stack boxes, and move carts around people. Workers still pack orders, load trailers, perform quality checks, handle hiccups and exceptions, and keep the machines running when they fail.
For Amazon, the immediate payoff is not necessarily a war

articles.title_zh: This painting went missing 20 years ago. Police tracked it down with the help of AI
articles.content_orig:
Art theft is a global problem and police forces are struggling to keep on top of it. Now they are turning to AI software that snoop out the most cleverly hidden artworks.
During their routine visit to the annual antiquity fair in Parma , Italy, in October 2024, police officers busily snapped photos of the artworks as they walked between the stands. It wasn't art appreciation – it was detective work.
The images were uploaded to an internal database as the officers smiled at the vendors and wandered amid fist-sized bronze statuettes, patinated goblets, yellowing globes, and an endless assortment of oil paintings.
Just a couple of hours later, though, the police system flagged one of the snapshots with an alert signal: a painting of a young, fair-skinned woman wearing aquamarine and red, holding up a half-unravelled parchment scroll.
The next day, officers rushed to the scene and seized the painting for their art experts to take a second look. The scroll in the painting was now, indeed, giving the investigators reason to be suspicious, says Lt Col Salvatore Rapicavoli, of the police unit for the Protection of Cultural Heritage of Italy. "There was something off."
While Rapicavoli's team has specialised in tracking down stolen artworks nationwide for decades, he says that the novel, tailor-made artificial i ntelligence system they were testing at the fair has massively sharpened their craft. It has since allowed the team to detect stolen art more quickly and helped them to spot details beyond what the human eye can normally see.
"There has been an exponential increase in the number of hits," says Rapicavoli. Since its introduction in November 2023, the AI system has helped his team recover more than 300 large plundered paintings and statues, and more than 165,000 smaller coins, medals, letters, manuscripts, religious objects, stamps and cards worth more than a total of €203m (£170m, $226m). The advances in Italy – in technique and policy – have been paving the way for machine learning in art theft investigations worldwide , promising to revolutionise the global crackdown on art heisters.
And while a human would likely have glossed over that woman holding a parchment scroll at first glance – nothing but a couple of darker shadows looking off balance – the team now had an active investigation on their hands.
Since 1969, the Italian police have kept a database of looted cultural artefacts across the nation – everything from gigantic oil paintings ripped from church altars in the night to ancient Roman and Etruscan artefacts excavated illegally. The database – the largest in the world, constantly fed by reports from cultural police authorities and customs – contains more than one million items. Though only some of the entries have pictures of the original artefacts.
Historically, to find stolen artworks, Italian police routinely visited fairs, antique shops, and upscale art auctions and compared what they saw there with millions of records back in their offices, first in paper form, then digitised in an online database. One by one, they would look for matches in the online repository by searching keywords, querying with details like "painting of woman with scroll".
This was time-consuming and clumsy, though, says Rapicavoli. Even if a sale looked suspicious, an officer scrolling through hundreds of database photos for a match could often miss key details. And the quality of the original artefact photos left a lot to be desired. The images were often taken decades earlier, in black and white, far away, on someone's dining room wall and littered with light blowouts, obscured areas, or extreme contrast.
"I asked myself how technology could get around this problem," says Rapicavoli, an IT engineer who joined the Italian police's stolen art team in 2013. "At least in the massive search-and-comparison phase."
In 2020, his team conceived the AI algorithm called the Stolen Works of Art Detection System (Swoads). "The machine doesn't get bored," says Rapicavoli. Crucially, it can match hidden visual fingerprints in the works – pairing similarities between shades of colour and rough silhouettes.
It can also spot segments of paintings that have been chopped up and rearranged – as is often the case with large altarpieces sold in separate slivers – or works that have been tweaked after being stolen. "Regardless of whether it makes sense or not, it recognises it because it's part of a whole that was stolen," says Rapicavoli. It can reconcile the art without truly knowing its meaning or content.
A manual search for a painting of a "woman with a scroll" in the stolen artworks database wouldn't have solved the case on Rapicavoli's hands. The keywords wouldn't have surfaced the painting stolen 20 years earlier, in which that same fair-skinned woman clutches a small white lamb and a palm branch instead of a scroll.
Because the AI had spotted the similarities in colour, pattern and set-up – irrespective of the missing scroll – it flagged it among millions of stolen artefacts despite the manner of its disguise. Once it fetched the source image it believed it resembled, the similarities to the human eye were immediately apparent.
In fact, a closer investigation confirmed that a 17th-Century, 1m-tall (3.3ft) painting of Saint Agnese had been looted from the small church of Virgo Potens in Sulmona, near Naples, over 500km (310 miles) from the Parma art fair, on the night of 11 August 2004. It had apparently then been painted over to appear less recognisable – the lamb now the scroll, and the halo and the palm branch erased to turn the Saint into a young pagan woman instead.
As the art trade moved from in-person auctions to online marketplaces, Rapicavoli's team was finding itself constantly playing catch-up with a flurry of new uploads across e-commerce platforms, social media, and even the dark web. Now Swoads can continuously crawl catalogues and new uploads day and night, constantly scraping the internet and comparing millions of images against a stolen-art database.
In 2026, for instance, the same software allowed his team in the Italian city of Turin to recover a painting by Filippo Palizzi, Riposo Della Pastorella (The Rest of the Shephardess), stolen from a modern art gallery in June 1972, in a robbery so severe the establishment remained shut down for over 30 years.
Although the painting had been missing for decades, lost in the backrooms of art markets and trade shows, one of its routine trawls of the internet spotted it for sale on an auction house website.
Still, AI isn't a silver bullet against art theft, says Carina Popovici, the co-founder of Art Recognition, a company using AI for art authentication. These systems answer a specific question: does this image match something reported stolen? They don't catch the thief, and they can't flag something that was never recorded, she notes. "The recovery still depends on investigators and legal cooperation," says Popovici. "I would call AI a force multiplier."
Timothy Carpenter, the former head of the FBI's Art Crime Team, and founder of Argus Cultural Property Consultants, a risk management and consulting firm, agrees. The software can't replace human analytical thought.
For one, there are still many technical issues to iron out. While the technology has become much better at recognising stolen art even from low-quality photographs, it still struggles with poor training data. Its recognition of 3D objects, too, is severely impaired – a vase photographed from the front in the theft report will likely not match a listing photographed from the back. Rapicavoli's team is already working to improve this.
And there are systemic issues: "You have to have a large team dedicated to nothing but chasing leads generated by the AI," says Carpenter – a luxury most law enforcement branches cannot afford. "The Italians have somewhere in the neighbourhood of 300 personnel assigned to their art crime unit. At its largest, the FBI had 24."

articles.title_orig: Federal Reserve set to issue interest rate decision as midterm elections loom - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Federal Reserve set to issue interest rate decision as midterm elections loom - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Markets expect the central bank to hold rates steady for now.
The Federal Reserve is set to issue an interest rate decision on Wednesday as a surge of inflation puts pressure on central bankers to raise rates days before the midterm elections.
An acceleration of price increases this year has posed a challenge for Fed officials tasked with containing inflation. The central bank raised interest rates a quarter of a percentage point last month in an effort to battle back price woes. The move marked the first rate increase in three years.
The rate hike should help cool off inflation by slowing the economy and eating away at demand, though such a policy move typically yields results after a lag time lasting several months.
Policymakers may lose patience as they weigh whether the current level of interest rates is high enough to ease price hikes, though markets expect the central bank to hold rates steady for now.
Investors put the chance of the Fed holding rates steady on Wednesday at about 90%, according to CME Group’s FedWatch Tool , a measure of market sentiment.
The current policy stance may not stick for long, however. The odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in December are pegged at 75%, the tool shows.
In the meantime, price increases are accelerating. Inflation rose to a four-month high in September as fuel prices climbed in response to unrest in the Middle East, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
Prices increased 3.7% in September compared to a year earlier, putting the inflation rate more than a percentage point above the Fed's target level of 2%, data showed.
The rise of inflation may put pressure on the Fed to ratchet up interest rates in an escalation of its fight against price hikes. That policy would mean pressing the brakes harder on the economy -- risking sluggish growth and job cuts.
A weak jobs report this month complicated the economic picture, suggesting a resilient labor market may be wobbling more than previously thought.
Employers added 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp slowdown from the 162,000 jobs added in August, the BLS said. The job gains came in well below economists' expectations.
Economic conditions pose a quandary for the Fed, Bank of America Global Research said in a memo to clients last week.
"If the Fed hikes, investors might worry about overtightening. If the Fed holds, markets could question the Fed's inflation-fighting credibility," the memo said.
The Fed's benchmark interest rate currently stands between 3.75% and 4%. That level marks a significant drop from a recent peak attained in 2023, but rates stand well above a 0% level established at the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The rate decision may also thrust the central bank into a political maelstrom in the final sprint to Election Day.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized the Fed for raising interest rates over across both terms in office, including a reprimand leveled at the Fed soon after its rate increase last month.
"LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!" Trump said in a social media post hours after the announcement.
The Fed is an independent institution established by Congress. The central bank is typically insulated from political interference, but several past presidents have sought to influence the Fed’s interest rate policy, including Trump.
The rate decision may also draw attention to the challenge posed by inflation, a top issue among voters.
In a memo to clients, Deutsche Bank Research said the upcoming midterms could factor into a potential decision to hold interest rates steady, though in their view the election would not be a "primary consideration."
"We could imagine that all else equal the Fed might prefer to stay out of the headlines for raising rates just ahead of a midterm election where affordability is the principal concern," the memo said.

articles.title_orig: A US cruise ship suspends a global voyage in Asia due to fuel costs, stranding 200 passengers
articles.title_zh: A US cruise ship suspends a global voyage in Asia due to fuel costs, stranding 200 passengers
articles.content_orig:
A U.S. cruise ship on a residential world voyage has suspended its operations in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to abandon their homes
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- A U.S. cruise ship on a residential world voyage suspended its operations in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to abandon their floating homes.
The Odyssey set sail two years ago on a three-year voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel.
The Florida-based company said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 has recently reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia during the war in Iran. Villa Vie Residences said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surge in fuel costs.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” it said. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
Sihanoukville Autonomous Port said in a statement last week that the ship docked on Oct. 23 for a five-day visit. It was to head to Vietnam but remained in the port Wednesday.
The ship carried 203 passengers with 15 nationalities, mostly Americans, and 156 crew members. It had a capacity of 650 residents.
Passengers have been told to leave the ship, but the crew's status was unclear.
The Odyssey had a confirmed itinerary into November 2027. The company planned for a second residential cruise ship to enter service in early 2029, but the statement on the suspension of the Odyssey's voyage did not address the second ship.
This version has corrected the date when the voyage was expected to end from 2030 to 2027.

Oops, something went wrong
Seagate (STX) dropped 30% in a month yet posted record Q4 revenue of $3.63B, up 48%, with supply allocated into 2028.
Morgan Stanley made a bullish case for battered Seagate and Western Digital (WDC) shares, according to Barron's.
Seagate trades at 18x forward earnings versus Western Digital's 23x, despite nearly identical operating margins of roughly 43%.

On the July call, CEO Dave Mosley said "data center demand now represents approximately 90% of our exabyte shipments" and that most nearline exabytes are "allocated into calendar 2028." The selloff prices in a cycle peak that Seagate's contracts don't yet show.
Shares fell 7.86% on October 22, 7.05% over the week and 30.13% over the past month. They are still up 133.96% year to date. The stock sits 43.8% below its 52-week high of $1,143.27 and about 197% above its low of $216.39. Non-GAAP gross margin expanded to 52.7% from 37.9%. For fiscal Q1, management guided to revenue of $4.10B ± $100M and EPS of $7.30 ± $0.20.
HAMR technology is the growth engine. Exiting fiscal 2026, HAMR products made up about 40% of Seagate's nearline exabyte run rate. Mozaic 4, which supports up to 44 terabytes per drive, is scaling up with the two largest cloud providers. Mozaic 5 is on track for qualification shipments in late calendar 2027.
Because each disk holds more data, profit grows without adding factory output. Management said incremental gross margin is "well above the 60% figure." Agentic AI could add more demand as KV cache data spills onto hard drives, and so could physical AI, though Mosley called both "very early days."
Wall Street mostly agrees: 4 Strong Buys, 18 Buys, 2 Holds and 1 Strong Sell. The bull case hits $1,201.97, an 87.18% gain.
Hard drives have a long history of boom-and-bust cycles, and Seagate depends heavily on a small group of hyperscalers whose capex plans drive the whole order book (we profiled seven of the non-chip suppliers riding that same expansion, from power to cooling to storage, in a free report).
Other risks include dilution from the Exchangeable Senior Notes due 2028, tariffs, exposure to the Middle East conflict and settlement payments to the Commerce Department's BIS. Still, contracts set product configuration and pricing for all of calendar 2027, and Seagate paid down $1.40B of debt. The bear case sits at $614.24, a decline of just 4.34%.
Western Digital is the other half of the HDD duopoly. In fiscal Q1, its revenue grew 55.46% and non-GAAP gross margin hits 58.1%. It trades near 23x forward earnings, compared with our about 18x for Seagate.
Micron Technology ( NASDAQ:MU ) gives a memory-side contrast. At about 7x forward earnings, it shows how cheaply the market prices AI hardware it views as cyclical.
Seagate's margins are almost the same as Western Digital's, yet it trades at a lower multiple. That makes the 24/7 Wall St. price target look reasonable, and arguably conservative.
The 24/7 Wall St. price target of $794.02 carries a buy rating and 90% confidence. The critical factor is supply that is already allocated into 2028.
The thesis improved if fiscal Q1 results land near guidance and Mozaic 4 hits its milestones. It weakens if hyperscalers start shortening their planning horizons. Those are the signals to watch from here.

The outlook depends on Seagate keeping its HAMR roadmap on track. A sharp cut in hyperscaler capex is the biggest downside risk, while demand from agentic and physical AI is the biggest source of upside.

articles.title_orig: Ten people confirmed dead in high-speed Spain train crash, local media report
articles.title_zh: Ten people confirmed dead in high-speed Spain train crash, local media report
articles.content_orig:
At least 10 people have been killed in a collision between two trains in the Spanish province of Toledo, it was reported on Wednesday.
The high-speed trains collided shortly before 9:15 a.m. local time (4:15 a.m. ET), when emergency services were deployed to the scene.
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, told Spanish broadcasters that the incident had resulted in at least 10 deaths.
Authorities said they would open the town of Urda's sports hall to provide assistance to those affected, with an Advanced Medical Post being set up at the site of the crash to triage the injured, provide medical care and transfer those requiring further treatment to hospitals. It is currently unclear how many people suffered injuries.
Railway infrastructure manager Adif is investigating the sequence of events surrounding the accident, Spanish news agency EFE reported on Wednesday.
Adif said in a post on X on Wednesday morning that traffic on the Madrid to Andalucía high-speed line had been interrupted due to a collision between two trains.
Newspaper El Pais reported that officials fear the number of confirmed fatalities may rise, with sources telling the outlet that Wednesday's collision could have a worse outcome than a high-speed crash in southern Spain that killed 45 people earlier this year.
"We don't have a figure, but it's going to be a major tragedy," Spain's Health Minister Mónica García told a television news station, according to El Pais.
Officials currently do not know for certain what caused the collision on Wednesday, but local reports said initial analyses pointed to human error. Government sources told El Pais that it appeared an Adif operator made a mistake when railway signaling systems failed. The systems are automated, but they rely on manual operation when signals fail.
The trains involved were operated by AVE and Iryo, according to local media, with at least two carriages said to have fallen down an embankment after the crash. More than 500 passengers were on board the two trains, El Pais said.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said in a post on X that he was "shocked" by the accident.
"Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations," he said, according to a translation. "My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families."
Sanchez's political future will be tested in a snap election next month, which he called following widespread unrest over Spain's housing crisis.
Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right Vox party — which is expected to make gains when Spain goes to the polls — pointed the finger at Sanchez's government over the train accident on Wednesday.
"Tragedy again. Rage again over the neglect, the ruin, and the betrayal suffered by the Spanish people," he said in a post on X.
